title: Comment from Kertzman, Andrew
printtext:
In the 2016 final rule economic analysis, OSHA estimated an annualized cost of the final rule would total $305 million (81 FR 82847). OSHA estimated that retrofitting fixed ladders between 24 feet and 30 feet in height with ladder safety and personal fall arrest systems would total $8.5 million in aggregate costs, for the approximately 109,200 fixed ladders OSHA stated would be affected.

OSHA's estimation of the number of affected ladders, and associated costs are divorced from reality. OSHA published "Impacts Exhibit V-1: Estimated Annualized Costs and Benefits of the Final Rule" Explicitly states in the last row the "More stringent Alternative - Mandated Combination of Cages, Wells, Landing Platforms, and Ladder Safety Systems" has "Modestly Higher Benefits (...)" for "Significantly Higher Costs (Possibly over $1 Billion). There is no difference in policy or effect between what OSHA promulgated, and OSHA's "more stringent alternative" described in the preamble (The more stringent alternative would require that employers provide cages, wells, landing platforms, and ladder safety devices for all fixed ladders; the cost of this alternative would be highly significant, while the incremental benefits would be modest relative to the preferred alternative.) OSHA promulgated a "more stringent alternative" policy, while disingenuously claiming "preferred alternative" costs in it's economic analysis.

Many of the sources below are cited in the final rule.
Commercial Buildings Energy Consumption Survey
Dept of Defense, Base Structure Report
US Census Bureau, American Housing Survey
US Energy Information Admin, Manufacturing Energy Consumption Survey

Numbers of buildings in the US are provided below from these sources.
~800,000 warehouse/storage buildings,
~400,000 religious buildings,
~400,000 education buildings,
~400,000 food service buildings,
~1,700,000 two story or greater commercial buildings,
~30,000,000 two story or greater residential buildings

OSHA conservatively estimates of the more than ~34 million two story or greater buildings in the US, around 0.3% are affected. Both the quantity of affected ladders in the US, as well as the associated costs of the rule are off by no less than two orders of magnitude.

OSHA heavily sourced all of their numbers and costs from the Eastern Research Group "Technical and Analytical Support and Docket Review for OSHA's Preliminary Analysis of Costs, Benefits, and Economic Impacts for OSHA's Proposed Standard for Walking and Working Surfaces.", but the numbers are +20-30 years old and don't account for growth/inflation.

Many supported scaffolding systems (not even identified in OSHA's 2016 economic analysis) use fixed external ladders, and are used not just in construction sites, but also building and equipment maintenance activities in fixed industry establishments covered by the rule. If these are assembled onsite, the associated ladders would be "built/assembled" after the 2016 final rule, requiring anchorages/SRLs, etc.

OSHA's identified economic feasibility burdens fundamentally relies on fixed ladders having a 20 year lifespan, when in truth if maintained in good condition and regularly inspected have a potentially indefinite lifespan. If a fixed ladder with cage was installed indoors in a warehouse the year before OSHA's 2016 rule was promulgated, and then only used 20 or 40 times, and was still in pristine condition; OSHA would burden that employer with the cost of disposing of the ladder and replacing it something engineered to support a ladder safety system.

Lastly, and most importantly; nearly all of the costs of compliance with the final rule are tied to this particular element, and the preamble to the 2016 final rule doesn't even attempt to represent how many lost work days or fatalities are specifically tied to falls from fixed ladders with cages. In 2020, only 5 deaths and ~5% of ladder fall injuries and illnesses are associated with fixed ladders compared to portable ones. As close as makes no difference to all ladder risks are associated with the portable ones; and OSHA requires zero fall protection on portable ladders whatsoever. The reason OSHA doesn't provide fixed ladder specific injury/illness numbers is BLS data mostly isn't/wasn't that granular. In OSHA's 2016 final rule fixed ladder risks and costs are comingled with portable ones, likely in an effort to lend justification to the fixed ladder requirements which are untenable on their own. As a result, all of the portable ladder injuries/illnesses will occur unimpeded, while all of the economic burden gets shifted to facilities with fixed ladders.

title: Anonymous Public Comment
printtext: Nearly a decade ago, a close family member of mine was working in construction when he fell off of an unsecured roof, and severely injured his shoulder while trying to catch himself on the way down. A lifelong manual laborer, he has been unable to find solid work years afterwards, and is still struggling with the effects of this injury today. Even within the status quo, professions that are reliant on ladders rank among the most dangerous, with OSHA listing “Roofers” and “Helpers in Construction Trades” as the second and fourth most dangerous jobs in the United States respectively, and furthers that the leading cause of fatalities for both is falls. In 2021 for example, falls accounted for 37% of construction site fatalities. As such, it seems incredibly inadvisable to not just maintain the status quo, but to take action to specifically remove safety measures, which is exactly what this rule change would do. There’s a reason this regulation was put in place to begin with: ladder cages are simply not safe enough. They do nothing to break or even slow a fall should one occur, and simply direct you downwards to your death instead of outwards toward your death. Furthermore, beyond the obvious lack of a safety system, this rule change would actually encourage workplaces to continue using increasingly unsafe, aging ladders. According to Ladders UK Direct, the upper end of a lifespan for a commercial ladder is about 20 years. This rule was first implemented in 2016, which is 20 years before the 2036 deadline. Under this rule change, if employers replace a ladder that is currently in place, they will still need to equip the new one with a personal fall arrest system. In other words, once employers are approaching the 2036 deadline, they will almost certainly be required to implement a personal fall arrest system regardless of the deadline. Therefore, since there is no longer a blanket deadline, employers will be incentivized to use potentially unsafe, past-lifespan ladders to avoid these requirements. OSHA is seeking comment on both the currently proposed deadline removal, and the potential repeal or revision of the requirement at large. Both of these changes would be egregiously bad ideas, and I would further say that given the poor safety conditions of these workplaces in the status quo, more safety regulations are needed, not less. The entire purpose of OSHA, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, is to ensure good safety and health practices are being followed in the workplace. Changing this regulation will lead to nothing but unnecessary hazard, injury, and even death in the workplace. I urge you not to finalize this change.

title: Comment from Henn, Daniel
printtext:
Regarding the petition submitted by the American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers (AFPM), American Chemistry Council (ACC), and the American Petroleum Institute (API), which seeks to dilute the requirements established in 29 CFR §1910.28(b)(9): I oppose this petition and reject the propositions asserted therein.
To begin, the negotiation of fixed ladders which are unprotected by ladder safety systems or personal fall arrest systems is a pervasive hazard for the American worker. The sheer verticality of these ladders requires the worker to negotiate them at an unnatural angle requiring physical effort to not only climb the ladder, but to remain adhered to the ladder as well.
BLS data published over the last ten years illustrates that 40% of all fatal fall occurs in fall distances of 15 feet or less, and in this respect, the regulation is generous in that it only targets ladders of 24 feet or greater. Furthermore, it is important to note that this same data suggests that one out of six fatal falls is ladder related. I concede that this data is heavily contaminated by incidents involving portable ladders as well, but when we consider that the ten-year trend of fatal occupational falls shows that the number of SIF incidents for workers at height is increasing or remaining stable; occupational fatalities overall are decreasing over time. It is clear to those of us engaged in mitigating fall hazards that not enough is being done to protect workers at height. The increasing median days away from work for those involved in non-fatal fall incidents helps to emphasize this point as well.
I would also add that the financial impact of complying with the rule was wildly inflated in the petition, estimated to be approximately $54,000 per ladder, on average. Many of these hazards could easily be remediated with commercially accessible solutions on a self-performing basis at a cost of $1,000 - $3,000 per ladder. Even with the full burden of third-party qualified person involvement, procurement, engineering, installation, certification, etc. – the $54,000 per ladder figure is exaggerated by a factor of three to five times what it would cost for a more financially burdensome, outsourced approach.
Cages and wells are not functionally effective preventative measures and cannot prevent or effectively arrest a fall in a predictable or repeatable fashion. Such an assertion ignores the many developments in fall protection methods and technologies that have been developed to effectively mitigate hazards such as these since Subpart M was implemented back in 1994. It ignores 32 years of progress and evolution in the field of occupational height safety in favor of archaic methods that do little if anything to protect the people doing the work that makes the existence of the AFPM, ACC and API possible.

title: Comment from Wing, Josh; Valcourt Group
printtext:
(1) Introduction
I work in the commercial real estate industry, supporting building owners and operators across a large portfolio comprising thousands of workers. My role involves assisting with OSHA compliance, as well as overseeing fall protection system installations, inspections, and repairs. Through this experience, I regularly evaluate fixed ladder systems and advise on regulatory requirements, giving me direct, practical insight into how these standards are interpreted and applied in the field.
________________________________________
(2) Background
This comment pertains specifically to 29 CFR §1910.28(b)(9), which addresses fall protection requirements for fixed ladders that extend more than 24 feet above a lower level. The regulation outlines when ladder safety systems or personal fall arrest systems are required and clarifies the phase-out of cages and wells as compliant fall protection for new installations.
________________________________________
(3) Analysis
In practice, there is widespread misunderstanding within the commercial real estate market regarding the applicability of this regulation. Many building owners incorrectly believe that fixed ladders under 24 feet in height require ladder fall protection systems or cages. This misinterpretation leads to unnecessary installations and added costs without corresponding safety benefits.
Based on our portfolio of serviced buildings, which includes thousands of fixed ladders, only approximately 10%–20% meet the threshold requiring ladder safety systems under §1910.28(b)(9). The remaining ladders fall below the 24-foot trigger and do not require such systems under current OSHA standards.
This confusion appears to stem not from deficiencies in the regulation itself, but from a lack of clear understanding and consistent interpretation in the field. As a result, building owners are often overcorrecting, implementing systems that exceed regulatory requirements. This can divert resources away from higher-risk safety improvements and create inefficiencies in compliance planning.
Importantly, the regulation as written appropriately targets higher-risk scenarios—namely, longer ladder climbs such as those found on water towers and similar structures—where fall protection systems provide meaningful risk reduction. Applying these requirements to shorter ladders does not proportionally enhance worker safety and may dilute focus on more critical hazards.
________________________________________
(4) Recommendations
I recommend maintaining the current structure and thresholds outlined in §1910.28(b)(9), as they effectively balance safety and practicality. However, I strongly encourage OSHA to provide additional clarification and outreach to address common misinterpretations in the market. Specifically:
•Issue clearer guidance or interpretive materials emphasizing that the 24-foot threshold is the trigger for fall protection requirements on fixed ladders.
•Reinforce that cages are not required for ladders under 24 feet and are no longer considered compliant fall protection for new ladders exceeding that height.
•Consider publishing practical examples or industry-specific FAQs to help building owners and compliance professionals better understand when systems are—and are not—required.
________________________________________
(5) Conclusion
The current regulation under §1910.28(b)(9) is well-structured and appropriately focused on higher-risk ladder applications. In my experience, the primary issue is not the rule itself, but widespread misinterpretation leading to unnecessary compliance measures. Maintaining the existing regulation while improving clarity through guidance and education will better support building owners, reduce unnecessary costs, and ensure that safety resources are directed where they are most effective.

title: Anonymous Public Comment
printtext:
I strongly believe the regulation should remain in force exactly as written because the rule was created to protect workers. These workers routinely climb towers, monopoles, rooftops, and other elevated structures in high-risk environments, and having this rule in place continues to protect their health and safety. OSHA’s final Walking-Working Surfaces rule was published on November 18, 2016, and the expected service life of a fixed ladder system is 15-20 years, depending on environmental factors. This rule established a 20-year phase-in period for these ladders which would end in 2036, which aligns with the expected timeline of the natural lifecycle of these ladder systems.

Any fixed ladder installed immediately before the 2016 rulemaking would be at or near the end of its useful life by the 2036 deadline. At a minimum, those systems would reasonably be expected to require substantial inspection, corrosion mitigation, structural repair, or full replacement to remain safe for continued use. This makes the existing implementation schedule both technically reasonable and economically predictable for employers.

Falls remain the leading cause of death in construction, consistently accounting for the largest share of fatal occupational injuries year after year. OSHA continues to identify falls as one of the “Fatal Four” causes of construction deaths, underscoring that preventing falls from height remains one of the most effective ways to save lives on the job. Choosing to help save people's lives and prevent further injury should be the priority of OSHA.

For these reasons, I believe the current rule language and compliance deadline should stand unchanged.

Regarding the proposed removal of the November 18, 2036 deadline for fixed ladder replacement, I support the vacating of this obligation. The costs are excessive and the incidents are too infrequent to compel this replacement.

The obvious best practice is to have fall arrest or ladder safety systems in place; however, allowing extant ladder equipment to serve through the end of the useful life of the equipment will facilitate flexibility and preclude burdensome and onerous obligations on the part of employers.

The government compelling an action by an independent and private company is counter to the nature of this country. Many such cases. title: Comment from Schatz, Gabriel
printtext:
In their own words, OSHA’s main goal is to “provide safe and healthful working conditions for American workers,” and in order to continue to do so effectively, I firmly stand behind the notion of maintaining the established regulation deadline.
The original rule that was established in Walking-Working Surfaces (2016) enacted this deadline because OSHA knew that cages and wells were not enough to prevent deaths and injuries from falls. Rightfully so, considering that according to the CDC, in 2020 alone, there were almost twenty-three thousand workplace injuries involving ladders and over 160 deaths. With fall arrest or other safety systems in place, we significantly improve workplace conditions and protect workers from injury if a fall does inevitably occur.
Working on repair sites and around individuals who have twenty-plus years of experience, I have seen firsthand and heard countless stories about the dangers associated with a reluctance to comply with workplace safety. Rules like this are in place not to maliciously increase the financial burden of those who must meet compliance, but to maintain the safety of the American workers who have no other avenue of protection. OSHA has already established that worker safety is reliant on full compliance with this rule, and the deadline that is at risk of being eradicated embodies the procedural implication of this rule, not some optionality that implies a trivial basis of the argument.
If we allow the removal of this deadline, we are critically weakening any future prospects of complete compliance with the rule. The deadline should continue to be maintained as it effectively ensures a firm point of completion, not to mention the fact that it works to combat against the vagueness that “end-of-life replacement” presents with indefinite deferment. Without it, this vagueness opens up avenues that can prove to be harmful to workers who are left at the mercy of employers who have deferred this obligation of safety to their next most convenient moment.
This is not only a failure in regard to safety and operations, but a failure to the people and families whose lives have been lost or forever changed due to avoidable workplace deaths. OSHA has even stated that the current cages do not prevent falls; in fact, they can actually increase the severity of the injuries sustained during falls. Going even further, falls are cited as one of the leading causes of workplace-related deaths by OSHA, with fixed ladders being at the center of most incidents. The unavoidable truth is that this deadline can help enforce a rule that is projected to save almost thirty lives a year and thousands of injuries. It is the only action to take; alternatively, the removal of this deadline will undoubtedly undermine OSHA’s own safety projections, something that seems to actively work against its mission of safety.
Essentially, this action can be boiled down to a core cost-driven justification of action rather than a safety-driven administrative improvement. If the goal really is to simply provide increased flexibility and reduce the compliance burden, then establish a new deadline or create a broader scope of compliance. Simply removing the deadline is not the answer.
The original rule was crafted as a thoughtful response to persistent workplace fatalities; finding something that could stop the falls instead of redirecting them was a game-changer. However, this move to abolish the deadline tarnishes the original intent of the rule. Employers were never told nor expected to retrofit their ladders overnight; they were simply told to provide their workers with safer equipment that could help save lives. But now, as the compliance window shrinks with every passing day, the deadline is being questioned. Not because it was an action that was rushed or enacted without enough time to reflect, but because employers must soon begin taking action to better the conditions for their workers. The deadline eliminates this problem, while employers flirt with a delayed compliance loophole, and undoubtedly continue to use the old infrastructure well beyond the originally intended replacement date, the deadline presents a firm avenue to safety.
This move is nothing more than a corporate incentive push disguised as a break for employers who don’t need one. With no deadline, employers aren’t burdened with a fixed retrofit deadline, and in turn are not required to spend any money. Safety becomes a game of cost-benefit, where repairs are preferable to safer replacements, and upgrades are deferred indefinitely. OSHA enforcement becomes a metric of unpredictable case benefit, and it all happens at the expense of the worker. Workers are the ones stuck dealing with old, unsafe equipment and unreliable safety equipment improvements. The risk is now constant for workers, while the cost obligation becomes flexible for employers, and the cycle continues.

printtext: I support OSHA’s goal of standardizing safety color codes to make hazard identification clearer in shipyards. However, I recommend adding flexibility for real-world conditions. title: Comment from Jonas, Carsten
printtext:
I strongly support this proposed rule. Removing standards that address hazards covered by building and fire codes helps avoid confusion and inadvertent violations that can easily occur when the codes are inconsistent with OSHA standards.

Many OSHA standards were enacted decades ago. Building and fire codes have significantly evolved since then, often at a much faster pace than OSHA standards. Additionally, the pace at which states and local jurisdictions adopt new editions of building and fire codes varies significantly throughout the US.

When two sets of prescriptive regulations (OSHA standards, and building and fire codes) both address the same hazard, this can easily lead to confusion and inadvertent violations.

I believe it would be advisable for OSHA to review its other standards as well to identify standards that address hazards covered by building and fire codes, and to repeal those standards (thus using the General Duty Clause to address those hazards) or replace their prescriptive requirements with performance-based objectives, which can easily be used in connection with any version of a building or fire code without hindering innovation.

Some people might be concerned about what this would mean for the few (mainly rural) jurisdictions that have not adopted building or fire codes and are in a state without statewide code adoption. However, even if the codes are not adopted into law in a jurisdiction, they can still be used as a benchmark to assess the safety of a workplace in relation to hazards covered by the codes.

In conclusion: this proposed rule is an excellent starting point to fostering a cooperative relationship between OSHA standards and building and fire codes. I strongly encourage OSHA to not only move forward with this proposed rule but also work to repeal or modernize its other standards that are duplicative of building and fire codes.

title: Comment from Physicians for Human Rights
printtext:
Dear Commissioner Makary, 

On behalf of Physicians for Human Rights (PHR), we submit this comment in full support of citizen petitions FDA-2025-P-0377-0001; FDA-2025-P-1576-0001; FDA-2025-P-2162-0001 that, among other measures, request the FDA to refrain from imposing additional restrictions on mifepristone. Recently, PHR and over 370 health care workers and 1974 allies wrote to you voicing their concerns on the recently announced FDA review of mifepristone.1 This comment consolidates these submissions and echoes support for the safety of mifepristone and its continued approval by the FDA. 

 

The FDA’s initial approval of mifepristone, also known by the brand name Mifeprex and RU486, in 2000 was predicated on years of rigorous, evidence-based research demonstrating the overwhelming safety and efficacy of mifepristone in use. It is recognized by the World Health Organization as a core medication on the Model List of Essential Medicines due to its safety, efficacy, and importance to health systems worldwide.2 In addition to its use in combination with misoprostol to assist abortion, mifepristone has been approved for the treatment of Cushing syndrome under the brand name Korlym since 2012. It is also under investigational use in the United States and other countries for the treatment of mental health and neurological conditions such as depression, dementia, post-traumatic stress disorder, Gulf War syndrome, delirium, suicide, psychosis, catatonia, and cognitive deterioration; cancers – particularly breast cancer; endometriosis; and uterine fibroids. Prior, post-approval updates to mifepristone access and REMS scheduling have similarly echoed the consensus of the existing literature, which demonstrates, based on concrete data and thousands of patients' experiences, that delivery of mifepristone is overwhelmingly safe and integral to the health of thousands of Americans.  

 

PHR has conducted extensive research on the impacts of abortion bans on US patients and clinicians, including specifically assessing the effects of depressed access to Mifeprex. These findings, most recently published in the brief “Cascading Harms: How Abortion Bans Lead to Discriminatory Care Across Medical Specialties,”3 demonstrated the negative repercussions of mifepristone restrictions on reproductive and non-reproductive clinicians. More than 100 peer-reviewed clinical studies have been conducted on mifepristone to assess its long-term safety, all of which showed the drug to be safe and effective.4

 

As PHR5 and other coalitions of experts and reproductive health scientists6 have expressed, the methodology and conclusions of the Ethics and Public Policy Center (EPPC) report which the present review of mifepristone is based fails to meet the high evidentiary, transparency, and methodological standards required of objective, empirical research.7 In contrast to the non-transparent data, unsubstantiated conclusions, and skewed methodological framing of the EPPC, the FDA’s prescribing information cites the findings of 10 clinical trials with more than 30,000 patients which show that serious adverse effects occur in fewer than 0.5% of patients.8 Similar reviews and studies have found comparable rates in both in-person and telehealth delivery of mifepristone.9 

 

Periodic reviews of medication are a meaningful and valuable tool to ensure patient safety, but they must be grounded in established medical evidence and scientific rigor. Rejecting medical precedent and injecting partisan politics into this process not only foments disinformation and undermines public trust in American health care authorities but also directly harms patients who depend on mifepristone for safe, effective care. 

 

PHR and its medical partners echo the requests included in the four petitions referenced above to reject additional restrictions on access to mifepristone for reproductive and non-reproductive use in the United States. As experts and health care providers, we urge the FDA to support evidence-based standards and align its regulatory standards with established patient-centered care. 

 

Sincerely, 
Physicians for Human Rights

title: Comment from Sriha Srinivasan
printtext:
As a medical student, a young woman, and a future physician committed to providing reproductive health and abortion care, I strongly support the Citizen Petition urging the FDA to remove the remaining REMS restrictions on mifepristone.

My medical education has taught me that clinical care should be guided by evidence. Mifepristone has been used in the United States for decades, and its well-established safety record does not justify subjecting it to restrictions that create additional barriers for patients, pharmacies, and clinicians. Requirements that providers register with manufacturers, pharmacies undergo special certification, and patients sign a medication-specific agreement do not make abortion care meaningfully safer. They make it harder to provide and harder to access.

As a future abortion provider, I am particularly concerned about what these requirements mean for the next generation of physicians. Every additional hurdle between a qualified clinician and their patient has consequences, particularly for patients who already face geographic, financial, logistical, or social barriers to reproductive healthcare.

I also write as a young woman who could need this medication myself. There is something deeply consequential about learning how to care for patients while simultaneously watching evidence-based reproductive healthcare become more difficult for people my age to obtain. Patients seeking medication abortion deserve the same respect, autonomy, and evidence-based standards that we expect throughout medicine. They should not be singled out for exceptional requirements when the evidence does not support them.

The FDA has an obligation to regulate medications according to scientific evidence and demonstrated risk. Maintaining unnecessary restrictions on mifepristone when the evidence no longer warrants them undermines that principle and imposes real burdens on patients and healthcare professionals.

I urge the FDA to grant the petition and remove the remaining REMS requirements for mifepristone. As someone preparing to spend my career caring for patients, I want to practice in a healthcare system where medical decisions are governed by evidence, where clinicians can provide appropriate care without unnecessary barriers, and where patients are trusted to make decisions about their own bodies and futures.

Comments on the NRC's Proposed Modernization of Radiation Protection
In the current proposed rulemaking, the NRC proposes, as the first of its Major Provisions, to remove the ALARA requirements from 10 CFR Chapter I and replace them with a Graded Approach to Dose Management.
In the section entitled "Reconsideration of LNT and ALARA," the NRC states that it is not rejecting the Linear No-Threshold (LNT) model itself, but rather identifies problems with the way the LNT model has been implemented in practice. This position appears to be based on the recognition that, at present, there is no scientific consensus demonstrating the existence of a dose threshold below which stochastic effects can be stated with certainty never to occur.
Consequently, I find the proposed Graded Approach to Dose Management to be generally unconvincing. It appears to be an arbitrary revision intended primarily to preserve consistency with the current regulatory framework rather than to reflect advances in scientific understanding.
The NRC justifies its continued reliance on the LNT model by citing the fact that the INWORKS study and the Million Person Study currently being conducted by the NRC have not disproved the LNT hypothesis, that organizations such as the ICRP continue to endorse the LNT model, and that the National Cancer Institute (NCI), as referenced in SECY-12-0064 (2012), concluded that the LNT model cannot presently be rejected.
However, conventional statistical analyses used in cohort studies have important methodological limitations. Because these analyses are dominated by data from highly exposed individuals, increasing the amount of data alone will not invalidate the LNT model, nor will it allow the radiation risks associated with low-dose exposure to be evaluated appropriately. These statistical issues have recently been highlighted in the Journal of Radiological Protection (DOI: 10.1088/1361-6498/ae890f).

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-14208, NRC-2025-1140-0001, from Jack Hudson
printtext:
**Public Comment on Docket ID NRC-2025-1140**
**"Reforming and Modernizing the NRC's Radiation Protection Framework"**

To the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission:

I am writing to oppose the NRC's proposed rule to eliminate the "As Low As Reasonably Achievable" (ALARA) principle and replace it with a "graded approach to dose management," as published in the Federal Register on July 15, 2026 (Docket ID NRC-2025-1140).

For more than fifty years, ALARA has required licensees not merely to stay under legal exposure limits, but to actively minimize radiation exposure to workers and the public whenever it is reasonably practical to do so. That ongoing obligation to reduce exposure — not just to avoid crossing a ceiling — has been a meaningful safety margin, not regulatory ambiguity.

I have several concerns with this proposal:

1. **A ceiling is not a safety program.** Legal dose limits (100 millirem/year for the public, 5,000 millirem/year for workers) define the maximum permitted exposure, not a safe or optimal one. ALARA's value was in pushing actual practice well below that ceiling. Removing the requirement to keep minimizing exposure — even while leaving the ceiling unchanged — removes the incentive to do better than the legal minimum, and over time will likely raise real-world doses toward that ceiling.

2. **The science does not support removing the safety margin.** Radiation risk is understood to follow a linear no-threshold model, meaning there is no exposure level considered entirely risk-free. Reducing exposure below legal limits whenever reasonably achievable has been a rational response to that reality. Replacing it with a threshold-based approach abandons that precaution in favor of administrative convenience.

3. **The stated justification is cost savings, not safety.** The NRC's own regulatory analysis and public statements frame this change primarily in terms of reducing costs and easing licensing for new reactor designs. Regulatory clarity is a legitimate goal, but it should be pursued by clarifying how ALARA is implemented, not by eliminating the underlying obligation to minimize exposure.

4. **The impact falls on workers and the public, not the agency.** The people most affected by this change are nuclear plant workers, medical radiation workers, and members of the public living near NRC-licensed facilities — not the companies that benefit from reduced compliance costs. Any rule change of this magnitude should weigh that asymmetry heavily.

I urge the Commission to withdraw this proposal and instead pursue targeted improvements to ALARA's implementation — clearer guidance, standardized cost-benefit criteria, streamlined documentation — without abandoning the core principle of continuous exposure minimization.

Thank you for considering this comment.

Respectfully,
Jack Hudson

Bridgeville, De 19933

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-14208, NRC-2025-1140-0001, from Cathy Iwane
printtext:
1. Abandoning the protective LNT assumption

Removing reliance on the linear no-threshold model would weaken the basic public-health presumption that every avoidable radiation exposure carries some incremental risk and that cumulative exposures matter.

Ionizing radiation can damage DNA. At low doses, the risk to any one individual may be small and difficult to detect epidemiologically, but “difficult to measure” does not mean “safe” or “zero.” The National Academies’ landmark BEIR VII review concluded that the evidence is consistent with a linear relationship between radiation dose and solid-cancer risk, and that it is unlikely that a harmless threshold exists below which cancers are never induced. It found that even the smallest dose may produce a small increase in risk.

More recent evidence reinforces that conclusion. The 2023 multinational INWORKS study of nuclear workers found increasing solid-cancer mortality with prolonged, low-dose occupational exposure—approximately a 52% increase per gray, with confidence intervals excluding no effect. Childhood CT research published in The Lancet also found that cumulative doses of roughly 50–60 mGy were associated with substantially increased leukemia and brain-tumor risks.

Public-health consequence: abandoning the no-threshold precaution risks treating small exposures as inconsequential even though millions of small exposures across workers, families and surrounding communities can produce preventable cancers at the population level. Children, pregnant women and people with repeated or cumulative exposures are not adequately protected by an approach focused only on avoiding immediately observable injury.

2. Removing ALARA

ALARA—keeping exposure as low as reasonably achievable, considering economic and societal factors—is not a demand for zero radiation. It is the practical optimization principle that requires licensees to use reasonable shielding, containment, distance, monitoring, maintenance and release controls rather than merely operating immediately below a legal ceiling. The International Commission on Radiological Protection continues to identify optimization of protection as a central radiation-safety principle.

A dose limit and ALARA perform different functions:

A limit is the maximum permitted exposure.
ALARA requires reasonable efforts to remain below that maximum.
Removing ALARA can turn a protective ceiling into an operational target. It reduces the continuing incentive to prevent leaks, improve filtration and shielding, shorten worker exposure, investigate unnecessary doses and adopt affordable safety improvements.

This concern is especially serious because the proposal would also increase the radionuclide-emission constraint from 10 mrem to 25 mrem per year, permit requests for public doses exceeding 100 mrem per year in some circumstances, and eliminate the existing two-mrem-per-hour public dose-rate provision.

Public-health consequence: exposures that are technically below a limit but reasonably preventable may be allowed to occur. Radiation-induced cancer is stochastic: the probability, not necessarily the severity, increases with dose. Waiting until a fixed limit is approached or exceeded is therefore not an adequate disease-prevention strategy.

3. Counting industry savings without quantifying health costs

The NRC prominently quantifies annual savings of approximately:

$9.53 million for industry
$244,000 for Agreement State regulators
$704,000 for the NRC
Yet the Federal Register summary provides no corresponding quantified estimate of additional cancers, medical expenses, lost income, premature deaths, genetic or developmental consequences, environmental monitoring burdens, or costs transferred to exposed families and communities.

That is a serious imbalance. The NRC itself calculates that raising continuous exposure from 10 to 25 mrem annually would raise estimated excess fatal-cancer risk from approximately 3.5 per 10,000 people to 8.7 per 10,000 people exposed for 70 years—about two-and-a-half times the estimated radiation-attributable risk. The agency calls both numbers small, but a small individual risk multiplied across large populations and generations is a real public-health burden.

Public-health consequence: the proposal presents regulatory and industry savings as concrete benefits while leaving possible health damage largely unpriced. The result can appear economically favorable only because cancer treatment, caregiving, disability, premature mortality, environmental contamination and loss of public trust are externalized onto the public.

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-14208, NRC-2025-1140-0001, from Kelley Boltin
printtext:
The ALARA principle—“As Low As Reasonably Achievable”—is a foundational concept in radiation protection, emphasizing the minimization of exposure to ionizing radiation through a balanced, risk-informed approach. Rooted in the Linear No-Threshold (LNT) model, which assumes no safe dose of radiation, ALARA is supported by major regulatory and scientific bodies including the NRC, ICRP, IAEA, OSHA, and FDA.

ALARA functions as an optimization strategy, aiming to reduce radiation exposure while considering technological feasibility, economic cost, and societal factors. It is embedded in national and international regulations and is upheld as both a legal requirement and an ethical obligation grounded in principles of beneficence, non-maleficence, justice, and autonomy.

Despite recent proposals—such as the NRC’s 2026 initiative to remove ALARA from its regulations—experts warn that eliminating ALARA could undermine safety, public trust, and regulatory compliance. Critics argue that ALARA can be overly conservative or economically burdensome, especially at low doses, but proponents emphasize its role in managing uncertainty and ensuring transparent, defensible decision-making.

ALARA is widely applied across sectors, including healthcare (e.g., diagnostic imaging, radiation therapy), nuclear power, industrial radiography, and research. Core implementation strategies include minimizing time near sources, maximizing distance, and using shielding, supported by training, monitoring, and technological innovations like robotics and AI-driven imaging.

Economic analyses show that ALARA-based programs often yield net benefits by reducing health risks, avoiding regulatory penalties, and enhancing public confidence. Rather than discarding ALARA, the report advocates for its modernization through explicit cost-benefit analysis, stakeholder engagement, and integration with performance-based regulations.

In conclusion, ALARA remains a critical, adaptable, and ethically grounded framework for radiation safety. Its continued application and evolution are essential to protect individuals, ensure regulatory integrity, and uphold societal trust in the use of ionizing radiation.

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-14208, NRC-2025-1140-0001, from Hiroto Kawakami
printtext:
Comments on the NRC's Proposed Modernization of Radiation Protection
In the current proposed rulemaking, the NRC proposes, as the first of its Major Provisions, to remove the ALARA requirements from 10 CFR Chapter I and replace them with a Graded Approach to Dose Management.
In the section entitled "Reconsideration of LNT and ALARA," the NRC states that it is not rejecting the Linear No-Threshold (LNT) model itself, but rather identifies problems with the way the LNT model has been implemented in practice. This position appears to be based on the recognition that, at present, there is no scientific consensus demonstrating the existence of a dose threshold below which stochastic effects can be stated with certainty never to occur.
Consequently, I find the proposed Graded Approach to Dose Management to be generally unconvincing. It appears to be an arbitrary revision intended primarily to preserve consistency with the current regulatory framework rather than to reflect advances in scientific understanding.
The NRC justifies its continued reliance on the LNT model by citing the fact that the INWORKS study and the Million Person Study currently being conducted by the NRC have not disproved the LNT hypothesis, that organizations such as the ICRP continue to endorse the LNT model, and that the National Cancer Institute (NCI), as referenced in SECY-12-0064 (2012), concluded that the LNT model cannot presently be rejected.
However, conventional statistical analyses used in cohort studies have important methodological limitations. Because these analyses are dominated by data from highly exposed individuals, increasing the amount of data alone will not invalidate the LNT model, nor will it allow the radiation risks associated with low-dose exposure to be evaluated appropriately. These statistical issues have recently been highlighted in the Journal of Radiological Protection (DOI: 10.1088/1361-6498/ae890f).
I therefore recommend that the NRC use data from the Million Person Study to perform an analysis similar to that presented in the above paper, in order to obtain a more accurate understanding of radiation risks in the low-dose region before finalizing the proposed revisions. I hope that the final rule will reflect both the results of cohort analyses based on this methodology and the latest findings in medical epidemiology, thereby leading to regulations that are scientifically sound and broadly acceptable to the public.

Comment on Docket FDA-2025-P-2526-0001
As the petitioner in FDA-2025-P-2526-0001, I submit this supplemental comment to strongly reinforce the urgent need for the FDA to grant the petition in full: immediately ban mercury dental amalgam (or reclassify from Class II to Class III), mandate comprehensive patient disclosures of mercury risks, and require evidence-based safe removal protocols (e.g., IAOMT SMART).
Mercury dental amalgam contains ~50% elemental mercury, a potent neurotoxin that releases vapor continuously, posing cumulative risks especially to children, pregnant/nursing individuals, and those with genetic susceptibilities. The FDA's own 2020 recommendations advise avoiding amalgam in high-risk groups due to potential neurodevelopmental, renal, and immunological harms—yet the agency continues to permit its use in most children ≥6 and the general population, relying on ethically and scientifically flawed data including the Casa Pia Children's Amalgam Trial (NIH/NIDCR Grant U01-DE011894).
This trial exposed ~507 institutionalized Portuguese children (many wards of the state) to amalgam during neurodevelopment, overlapping the 2002 Casa Pia systemic child sexual abuse scandal (public exposure/convictions during enrollment/follow-up). Consent/assent was compromised by extreme coercion/undue influence in an abusive institutional environment; no independent advocates were appointed for wards as required by 45 CFR 46.409 (Subpart D protections). Primary conclusions (DeRouen et al., JAMA 2006) claimed "no significant adverse effects," but independent re-analyses reveal clear harms overlooked in aggregate data:

Dose-dependent renal biomarker changes (GST-α/π, albumin) and glomerular/tubular injury (Woods et al., Environ Res 2008; PMID 18721920).
Elevated urinary porphyrins indicating early heme biosynthesis disruption, most pronounced in younger children (Woods et al., J Toxicol Environ Health A 2009; PMID 19557617).
Dose-related kidney integrity markers and urinary mercury increases (Geier et al., Hum Exp Toxicol 2012/2013; PMIDs 21803780, 22893351).
Neurobehavioral deficits in genetically susceptible subgroups (CPOX4, BDNF Val66Met polymorphisms), especially boys (Woods et al., Neurotoxicology 2014; PMID 25109824).

These signals demonstrate foreseeable harms not adequately assessed or disclosed, violating 45 CFR 46.111 (risk minimization) and 46.116 (informed consent). I have submitted a formal complaint to OHRP (February 2026) requesting noncompliance determination, suspension of federal reliance on this data, and remedial coordination—further evidencing the ethical compromise embedded in FDA policy.
Continued reliance on Casa Pia contradicts evolving science, FDA's high-risk warnings, and U.S. obligations under the Minamata Convention (ratified 2013; global phase-down). The EU banned amalgam effective 2025–2026; over 30 countries have restricted/banned it. The U.S. lags dangerously, exposing millions (including vulnerable/low-resource groups) to preventable mercury exposure.
Granting this petition would:

Protect public health by eliminating the largest non-occupational mercury source.
Align U.S. policy with international standards and Minamata goals.
Mandate disclosures and SMART removal to prevent iatrogenic harm during extraction.
Restore trust eroded by decades of inaction on known risks.

I urge the FDA to act expeditiously: approve the petition without delay, reject reliance on ethically tainted studies like Casa Pia, and initiate rulemaking for a full ban/reclassification. Public comments supporting this petition (e.g., "I support banning mercury dental amalgam to protect vulnerable populations") further demonstrate broad concern.
Thank you for considering this critical matter. I am available for any questions or additional evidence (FOIA records, publications, etc.).
Respectfully,
Anita Tibau

Approximately 1 in 6 adults were estimated to have neurological disease. Fourteen major neurological disorders were analyzed including stroke, Alzheimer disease and other dementias, Parkinson disease, epilepsy, multiple sclerosis, motor neuron disease, migraine, tension-type headache, traumatic brain injury, spinal cord injuries, brain and other nervous system cancers, meningitis, encephalitis, and tetanus.2

Sensitivity/Allergy to Mercury (12%): This population includes individuals with documented hypersensitivity or allergy to mercury, which can manifest in various symptoms. Research indicates that sensitivity among the general population varies, with certain demographics, especially those with specific health conditions, exhibiting a higher risk upon mercury exposure.3,4

Kidney Disease (14%): Individuals with kidney disease are at a higher risk due to their compromised ability to excrete heavy metals like mercury. Studies have shown a significant correlation between dental amalgam exposure and elevated mercury levels in urine among children and adults with kidney impairment.5,6 The prevalence of kidney disease in the U.S. is around 14%.7

Women of Child-Bearing Age (20%): Women of child-bearing age, especially pregnant women, are particularly vulnerable to the effects of mercury. Research links amalgam exposure to adverse pregnancy outcomes, leading this population to be advised to limit mercury exposure to safeguard fetal development.8–16 One important issue to keep in mind is that the rate of unintended pregnancies is high and therefore occur in women who aren’t prepared or thinking about protections for themselves and their unborn children17,18.
